title: Introductions I: Before You Start and Making Entries
summary: Learn what this syllabus is for, what students need before they begin, and how entries, timetables and retakes work.

sections.h: Why choose this syllabus?
p: Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510) helps students understand and use English in real life. They learn to understand written and spoken English. They also learn to write and speak clearly about both familiar and less familiar topics.

Cambridge IGCSE is the most popular international qualification for 14 to 16 year olds. Students can choose from about 70 subjects. It is taught in over 4,500 schools in more than 140 countries. Universities and employers know and trust it.

b: Confident: uses a range of language to share ideas in writing and speaking.
Responsible: looks for chances to use and improve English.
Reflective: thinks about different opinions and answers politely.
Innovative: uses language in a creative way.
Engaged: tries different ways of learning and uses English in many situations.

sections.h: Before you start
p: Cambridge suggests that students have already studied an English as a Second Language course, such as the Cambridge Lower Secondary programme, or a national course at the same level. This is advice, not a rule.

The syllabus is planned for about 130 guided learning hours. Guided learning hours means the time a teacher spends teaching or guiding the student. Some students need fewer hours and some need more. It depends on local practice and on what the student already knows.

b: 130 hours over two school years is about 3 hours a week for 40 weeks each year.
A student who already speaks a lot of English at home may need fewer hours.
A student who is new to English may need extra lessons or extra practice at home.

sections.h: When can students take the exam?
p: Every Cambridge school belongs to one of six administrative zones. Each zone has its own timetable. You can see your timetable at www.cambridgeinternational.org/timetables.

Students can be entered in the June and November exam series. Schools in India can also enter students in the March series. Always check that you are using the syllabus for the year your students will take the exam. Private candidates can enter too, but only if the centre can run and mark the Speaking test and send the work to Cambridge for checking.

b: A school plans to teach for two years and finish in time for June. The students sit June.
A student who is not ready can wait and sit November.
A private candidate asks a school to help. The school must be able to record and assess the Speaking test first.

sections.h: Combining with other syllabuses and making entries
p: Students can take this syllabus together with other Cambridge syllabuses in the same exam series. There are a few exceptions. They cannot take it with Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0511) Count-in Speaking, IGCSE (9-1) English as a Second Language (0993 or 0991), IGCSE First Language English (0500), IGCSE (9-1) First Language English (0990), Cambridge O Level English Language (1123), Cambridge IGCSE English (as an Additional Language) (0472), or any syllabus with the same title at the same level.

Exams officers send the entries to Cambridge. Work closely with your exams officer so that the right students are entered for the right papers. Cambridge gives exams officers a Guide to Making Entries. It lists the entry option codes. The syllabus and all exam papers are in English only.

ex.t: Example: retakes and carrying marks forward
b: Students can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want.
Marks from Paper 3 Speaking can be carried forward to a later series. Check the Cambridge Handbook for the rules.
Students cannot send in a Speaking test from an earlier series again, in whole or in part.

activity: Write a one-page plan for your school. Include: how many guided learning hours you have, which exam series you will use, who your exams officer is, and the date you will talk to them about entries. Check the timetable for your zone first.

title: Introductions II: Accessibility, After the Exam and Using the Grades
summary: Understand access arrangements, how grades and results are reported, and how teachers and students can use the grades.

sections.h: Accessibility and equality: fair for all students
p: Cambridge tries to make its syllabuses and exam papers fair for students of every country, culture and background. The language and layout of papers are planned to be as easy to access as possible. This helps all students show what they know.

Even so, some students need extra help. Cambridge uses access arrangements for students with special educational needs (SEN), a disability, an illness or an injury. These follow the idea of reasonable adjustments in the UK Equality Act (2010). They remove barriers without making the exam easier.

ex.t: Example: who might need an access arrangement?
b: A student with a hearing problem may need a different way to take the Listening test.
A student with a broken writing arm may need help with writing.
A student with a reading difficulty may need a modified paper.

sections.h: Rules for access arrangements
p: Access arrangements must be based on evidence that the student faces a barrier. They should also match the way the student normally works at school. Cambridge must agree that the arrangement is a reasonable adjustment, has a reasonable cost and time, and does not harm the security of the exam.

Check what is available at the start of the course, not just before the exam. Read the Cambridge Handbook at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide. If you need something that is not on the standard list, contact Cambridge early. A student who cannot access part of the assessment may still receive an award based on the parts they completed.

b: In week one of the course, note any students who may need help.
Collect evidence, such as notes from teachers or reports.
Ask your exams officer to check the Handbook and apply on time.

sections.h: After the exam: grades and results
p: Students receive grades A*, A, B, C, D, E, F or G. A* is the highest and G is the lowest. Ungraded means the work did not reach the standard for grade G. Ungraded appears on the statement of results but not on the certificate.

Speaking is reported separately. Where students reach the right standard, the certificate shows a Speaking grade from 1 (high) to 5 (low). The Speaking marks do not change the written grade. Sometimes the statement of results shows Q (pending) or X (no result). These letters do not appear on the certificate. The certificate names the qualification as International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE).

b: Grade B in written papers and Speaking grade 2: two separate results on one certificate.
Grade C overall with Speaking grade 2: Cambridge says this can be seen as about level B2 on the Common European Framework (CEFR).
Q means the result is pending. X means no result.

sections.h: How students and teachers can use the grades
p: Assessment has two purposes. First, it measures learning and achievement. It confirms how well a student has shown the knowledge, understanding and skills in the syllabus. Second, it shows likely future success. Results help to predict who is well prepared for a course or a job. They help students choose the best course or career.

Teachers can use results to improve teaching. Look at which skills were strong and which were weak. Ask which papers need more practice next year. Cambridge gives teachers results analysis and examiner reports for this.

ex.t: Example: using results in a staff meeting
b: Listening results were lower than Reading. Plan more listening practice.
Many students lost marks on the formal writing task. Teach register and format.
Share the examiner report with colleagues and agree two actions.

activity: Choose one student (or an imaginary one) and write two lines for each: (1) an access arrangement that might help and the evidence you would collect, and (2) how you would explain the student's grade and Speaking grade to the parent.

check.q: Which grade is the highest at Cambridge IGCSE?

o: As a separate grade from 1 (high) to 5 (low)

o: At the start of the course

title: Syllabus Overview: Aims, Content, Assessment and Objectives
summary: See the big picture: the aims, what students learn, how the three papers fit together, and the sixteen skills that earn marks.

sections.h: Aims: what the course is for
p: The aims describe the purpose of any course based on this syllabus. The aims are to: develop students' ability to use English well for practical communication; develop their awareness of the nature of language and of how to learn languages; develop skills that help in other subjects; and support their personal development and enjoyment.
Keep these four aims on your wall. When you plan a lesson, ask: will this help the student use English in real life?

b: Practical communication: students leave a voice message to book a doctor's visit.
Awareness of language: students notice how a polite email differs from a text to a friend.
Transferable skills: students plan and present a short talk they can also use in Science.
Enjoyment: students choose a topic they care about for a speaking task.

sections.h: Content overview
p: The course builds practical skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking. Students read many kinds of text. They learn to pick out the right details, to tell what is stated from what is only suggested, and to write for different purposes and readers.

Students listen to talks and conversations. They speak about many topics and learn to answer in a way that fits the situation and the listener, with good accuracy and clarity. By the end, they should be independent users of English for further study and for daily life.

b: Topic: protecting the environment.
Reading: an article about plastic waste.
Writing: an email to a friend about a clean-up day.
Listening: a radio interview with a volunteer.
Speaking: a short talk on how to reduce waste at home.

sections.h: Assessment overview: three papers
p: Every student takes three components and can receive grades A* to G. Paper 1 is Reading and Writing. It takes 2 hours, has 60 marks and is 70 per cent of the written grade. It has six exercises: four reading and two writing. It is marked by Cambridge.

Paper 2 is Listening. It takes about 50 minutes, has 40 marks and is 30 per cent. It has five exercises and is multiple choice. It is marked by Cambridge. Paper 3 is Speaking. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes and has 40 marks. It is an interview, a short talk and a discussion. The teacher marks it and Cambridge checks the marks. Speaking is separately endorsed: it does not change the written grade.

ex.t: Example: the numbers at a glance
b: Paper 1: 2 hours, 60 marks, 70%.
Paper 2: about 50 minutes, 40 marks, 30%.
Paper 3: about 10 to 15 minutes, 40 marks, separately endorsed (grade 1 to 5).
There are no tiers in this version of the syllabus: all students take the same papers.

sections.h: Assessment objectives: the sixteen skills
p: Assessment objectives (AOs) are the skills the exam rewards. AO1 Reading: R1 understand specific facts; R2 understand how ideas, opinions and attitudes connect; R3 pick out details for a purpose; R4 understand implied meaning. AO2 Writing: W1 communicate information, ideas and opinions; W2 organise ideas with linking words; W3 use a range of grammar and vocabulary; W4 use the right register and style for the purpose and reader.

AO3 Listening: L1 specific information; L2 speakers' ideas, opinions and attitudes; L3 connections between them; L4 what is implied but not said. AO4 Speaking: S1 communicate ideas, facts and opinions; S2 control a range of vocabulary and grammar; S3 develop answers and keep talking; S4 control pronunciation and intonation. Weighting of the whole qualification: Reading 35 per cent, Writing 35 per cent, Listening 30 per cent. Speaking is separately endorsed. Inside Paper 1, Reading and Writing are 50 per cent each.

b: 'When does the festival start?' is R1 (a stated fact).
'What does the writer suggest about the town?' is R4 (implied meaning).
An informal email to a friend tests W4 (register) as well as W1 to W3.
Tell students the skill name before they practise. It helps them know what to do.

activity: Make a one-page poster for your classroom with the three papers (time, marks, per cent) on the left and the sixteen skills (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4, S1 to S4) on the right. Use your own simple words for each skill.

check.q: What share of the written grade is Paper 1 Reading and Writing?
Which objective is about understanding what is implied but not directly stated in a text?
How is Speaking (Paper 3) treated in the final result?
o: Separately endorsed with its own grade

title: Subject Content: Reading, Writing, Listening and Speaking
summary: See what students should be able to do in each skill, with clear examples and the text types they meet.

sections.h: Reading: what students learn to do
p: Students meet many kinds of text: instructions, notices, advertisements, leaflets, articles, blogs, reviews and web pages. The texts can describe, tell a story, give information, persuade, discuss or argue. Students should read widely in English, in class and at home.

They learn to find facts, to follow ideas, opinions and attitudes and the links between them, to understand what is implied, and to choose the right details for a purpose. They also learn reading strategies: skim reading (read fast to get the general idea), scanning (look for specific information) and careful reading (read slowly to understand detail). Good readers predict answers and notice what type of information a question wants.

ex.t: Example: three ways to read one blog post
b: Skim: read the title and the first line of each paragraph to learn what the post is about.
Scan: look for the date and the price when a question asks 'when' and 'how much'.
Read carefully: read the paragraph about the writer's feelings to answer an opinion question.
Guess a new word: read the sentences around it and decide what it probably means.

sections.h: Writing: what students learn to do
p: Students write for different purposes and different readers. They learn the features of each text type and are encouraged to plan, draft and check their work. They communicate facts, ideas and arguments clearly and add detail. They show control of grammar, vocabulary, punctuation and spelling.

They organise ideas in a logical order with paragraphs and linking words. For cause and effect they use words like therefore, because of, as a result and consequently. For adding ideas they use in addition, moreover and furthermore. For contrast they use however, in contrast, whereas and although. They use a range of grammar and vocabulary, such as different tenses, conditionals, phrasal verbs, collocations and idioms, and they avoid repeating the same word. They also choose the right register: informal for an email to a friend, more formal for a report, essay, review or article.

b: Informal (to a friend): 'Hi Sam! Guess what, I'm coming to your town next week. Fancy meeting up?'
Formal (to a teacher): 'Dear Mr Banda, I would like to ask whether I may hand in my essay on Friday.'
Teach students to ask: who is reading this and why am I writing?

sections.h: Listening: what students learn to do
p: Students listen to phone messages, announcements, radio programmes, TV, film, plays, news items, podcasts, conversations and interviews. These can be formal, semi-formal or informal. Students should listen to English widely in class and at home.

They learn to catch factual details such as places, names, times, dates and directions. They learn to understand speakers' ideas, feelings and attitudes, and the reasons behind them. They notice link words and pronouns. They work out what is implied and guess unknown words from the words around them. Before listening, they predict the type of information they will hear.

ex.t: Example: before, during and after listening
b: Before: read the question and decide if you need a name, a number, a place or a feeling.
During: write nothing long; listen for the key word and the link words such as but, so and because.
After: check that your answer matches what the speaker meant, not just a word you heard.

sections.h: Speaking: what students learn to do
p: Students speak in different situations: asking and answering in class, short exchanges, conversations, giving opinions and short talks. They practise functional language such as expressing preferences, telling a personal story, describing an experience, agreeing and disagreeing, giving advantages and disadvantages, and making predictions. Topics are everyday: the environment, health, food, film, travel, technology, celebrations, science, the arts and shopping.

They learn to expand answers by giving examples ('just to name a few'), giving reasons ('and that is why'), comparing ('just like', 'while'), speculating ('I suppose') and clarifying ('Sorry, I did not quite catch that'). They link ideas with discourse markers such as in addition, first of all, finally, that's why, however and although. They use a range of grammar and vocabulary and they paraphrase when they forget a word. They also work on pronunciation: word stress, sentence stress and rising and falling intonation.

b: Short: 'I like football.'
Expanded: 'I really like football, just like most of my friends. First of all, it keeps me fit, and that is why I play twice a week. However, I do not enjoy it when it rains.'
Teach students to add an example, a reason and a contrast.

sections.h: Glossary of text types
p: Article: a text for a general audience, for example in a magazine or newspaper, that informs or entertains. Blog: a text published on a website, usually informal. Conversation: a spoken exchange between two or more people, usually informal. Dialogue: any spoken exchange between two people. Email: electronic writing for a particular purpose, formal or informal. Essay: a text on a topic that gives an argument or point of view, with an introduction, main body and conclusion, and reasons or examples.

Instructions: a written or spoken text that tells you how to do something. Interview: a spoken exchange in which one person asks questions and the others answer. Leaflet: an informational text that explains or advertises something and is handed out. Monologue: a text spoken by one person only. Notice: a short written text with news or information, usually put on a wall or noticeboard. Report: a text for a superior or a group about an event, experience or situation, with facts and suggestions or recommendations. Review: a text for a general audience that describes and gives opinions about something the writer has experienced.

ex.t: Example: match the need to the text type
b: You want to tell a head teacher what happened at a school trip and suggest changes: report.
You want to give your opinion on a film you saw: review.
You want to tell a friend your news in a friendly way: informal email.
You want to inform people about a school event on a wall: notice.

title: Details of the Assessment: Paper 1, Paper 2 and Paper 3
summary: Walk through every exercise in the three papers: what students do, how many marks, and how Speaking is run and marked.

sections.h: Paper 1: Reading and Writing
p: Paper 1 is a written paper. It takes 2 hours and has 60 marks. It has six exercises: four reading and two writing. Students answer every question. Students write on the question paper. Dictionaries are not allowed. Reading uses multiple-choice, matching and some short answers in English.

Exercise 1 (8 marks): read a text of about 400 to 450 words. Five questions need one answer and the last needs three. Answers are single words or phrases. Exercise 2 (9 marks): multiple matching. Read a text of about 600 to 650 words in up to five sections, or up to five shorter texts, and match nine questions to the right section. Exercise 3 (7 marks): read about 400 to 500 words and complete brief notes. Exercise 4 (6 marks): read about 550 to 600 words and answer six multiple-choice questions with three options A, B or C.

ex.t: Example: reading marks at a glance
b: Exercise 1: 8 marks. Exercise 2: 9 marks. Exercise 3: 7 marks. Exercise 4: 6 marks.
Total for reading: 30 marks.
Skills tested: R1, R2 and R3 in all four exercises, with R4 in Exercises 2 and 4.

sections.h: Paper 1: the two writing exercises
p: Exercise 5 (15 marks) is an informal email. Exercise 6 (15 marks) is a more formal piece, such as an article, report, essay or review. In each, students write 120 to 160 words of continuous prose. They answer a short stimulus, which may include a picture, and short prompts. The stimulus tells them the purpose, format and reader, and these are different each time.

Each writing exercise is marked out of 15: up to 6 marks for Content (doing the task and developing ideas) and up to 9 marks for Language (range, accuracy and organisation). The skills tested are W1 to W4.

ex.t: Example: what to teach for the writing tasks
b: Read the task and underline the purpose, the reader and every prompt.
Plan three short points before writing.
Write 120 to 160 words: not much shorter, not much longer.
Check grammar, spelling and linking words in the last two minutes.

sections.h: Paper 2: Listening
p: Paper 2 takes about 50 minutes, including 6 minutes to copy answers onto a separate answer sheet. It has 40 marks and 40 multiple-choice questions in five exercises. Students hear every recording twice. Check the Cambridge Handbook for the year of the exam: it explains how to get the audio and how to set up the room, equipment and sound.

Exercise 1 (8 marks): eight short extracts, one question each, with four picture options A to D. Exercise 2 (10 marks): five short extracts, two questions each, with three written options. Exercise 3 (8 marks): one monologue (for example a talk) and eight sentences to complete with a word or short phrase from three options. Exercise 4 (6 marks): six short monologues in a multiple-matching task with eight statements to choose from. Exercise 5 (8 marks): an interview between two speakers and eight multiple-choice questions.

ex.t: Example: listening marks at a glance
b: Exercise 1: 8. Exercise 2: 10. Exercise 3: 8. Exercise 4: 6. Exercise 5: 8.
Total: 40 marks.
Skills tested: L1, L2 and L3 in all exercises, and L4 in Exercises 2, 4 and 5.

sections.h: Paper 3: Speaking
p: The Speaking test is about 10 to 15 minutes and is worth 40 marks. It is in English and must be recorded in full for every student. Dictionaries are not allowed. The teacher or examiner chooses one Speaking Assessment card for each student. The teacher conducts and marks the test, and Cambridge checks (moderates) the marks.

The test has five parts. Introduction (about 1 minute): start the recording, say your name, the student's number and name and the date, welcome the student and read the script. Not assessed. Warm-up (1 to 2 minutes): a short friendly chat. Not assessed. Part 1 Interview (2 to 3 minutes): a short interview on a topic. Assessed. Part 2 Short talk (3 to 4 minutes, with 1 minute to prepare): the student reads the card, prepares without writing notes, then talks alone. Assessed. Part 3 Discussion (3 to 4 minutes): questions linked to the Part 2 topic. Assessed.

b: Introduction and warm-up put the student at ease. They earn no marks.
Interview, short talk and discussion are the three assessed parts.
The student receives a card only for Part 2. The questions for Parts 1 and 3 are in the teacher's notes.
The whole test, from the start of the introduction to the end of Part 3, must be recorded.

sections.h: Marking Speaking, moderation and sending marks
p: Speaking is marked out of 40 on four criteria, each out of 10: grammar, vocabulary, development and pronunciation. Add the four marks for the total. The marks come from level descriptions from Level 5 (9 to 10 marks) down to Level 1 (1 to 2 marks), with 0 for no creditable response. Choose the best-fit level first. If the work convincingly meets the level, give the top mark. If it adequately meets it, give a middle mark. If it only just meets it, give the lowest mark.

Record marks on the Speaking Examination Summary Form, which you download each year from the samples database at www.cambridgeinternational.org/samples. The marks on the form must be the same as the marks you send. If more than one teacher marks Speaking in your school, you must standardise (internally moderate) the marking so that every student is judged to the same standard. Cambridge then externally moderates: you send the marks of all students and a sample of the marked work. Moderators write a short report with feedback for your centre.

b: Level 5: answers are relevant and consistently well developed; the student keeps talking with ease.
Level 4: answers are relevant and mostly developed; the student keeps talking with only a little support.
Level 3: answers are relevant with attempts at development; frequent support is needed.
Use the descriptors, not your feeling, to decide.
